title: Many voices, one Guru
hookLine: it holds hymns of six Gurus, fifteen Bhagats of many backgrounds, the Bhatt poets, and a few Sikhs of the Gurus' time
carry: a weaver's songs beside a king's

cards: A weaver's songs sit in the same book as a king's. A Muslim mystic from the Punjab and a Hindu poet from the east sing side by side.
A leatherworker, from a caste others of his time kept at a distance, even refusing to share water, has his hymns bowed to wherever the book is opened.
Sixteenth-century India was divided by caste and creed in ways that decided who could learn, who could pray where, who could even be touched.
Into that world, Guru Arjan put together a book, and he chose to fill it with many voices.

teach.b: Today's word is bani. It comes from an old word for speech, for voice. In Sikh use, bani means sacred utterance, the hymns themselves; gurbani means the Guru's word.
So whose bani does the Granth hold?
First, six of the Gurus: Guru Nanak, Guru Angad, Guru Amar Das, Guru Ram Das, Guru Arjan, and, added later by Guru Gobind Singh, Guru Tegh Bahadur.
Second, fifteen Bhagats, devotional poets from across India, several of whom lived before Guru Nanak. Kabir, the weaver of Banaras. Sheikh Farid, a Sufi Muslim saint of the Punjab.
Namdev, from a caste of tailors. Ravidas, a leatherworker. Sain, a barber.
Dhanna, a farmer. Pipa, who had been a king. Jaidev, a Brahmin poet.
Hindu and Muslim, high caste and low, in one book. Third, the Bhatts, bards who sang the praises of the Gurus. Fourth, a few Sikhs of the Gurus' own time, like the musicians Satta and Balwand.
Guru Arjan gathered these voices when he compiled the book; tradition dates it to 1604. Just as telling is where they sit. The Bhagats' hymns aren't an appendix.
They sit inside the ragas, beside the Gurus' own, and when Sikhs bow to the Guru Granth Sahib, they bow to Kabir's words and Farid's words too. All of it is honored as gurbani.
The voices are many. The Guru is one.

how: In gurdwaras, hymns by the Bhagats such as Kabir, Farid and Ravidas are sung in kirtan and read in the daily hukamnama just as the Gurus' hymns are, all honored as gurbani.

games.q: you're Guru Arjan, compiling the Granth in a world divided by caste and creed. whose hymns do you include?
o: the Gurus', and Bhagats of many backgrounds, Hindu and Muslim.
games.why: Guru Arjan included Kabir, Farid, Ravidas, Namdev and others, placing them inside the ragas, honored as gurbani.

practice: Let a few voices you trust come to mind, one at a time: a grandparent, a teacher, a friend, a writer, someone from a background very different from yours.
Choose one you'd want to hear more of, maybe someone you've overlooked, and hold their face in mind. Then let all the voices quiet down together, like a room settling before music begins.
